content: NRTI (Nucleos(t)ide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor): A class of antiviral drugs that inhibit the activity of reverse transcriptase, an enzyme critical for the replication of retroviruses such as HIV. OR (Odds Ratio): A statistical measure used to determine the strength of association between two events, often used in clinical research. OST (Opioid Substitution Therapy): A medical treatment for opioid dependence that involves replacing an illegal or harmful opioid with a medically supervised, safer alternative, such as methadone or buprenorphine. PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): A molecular biology technique used to amplify and detect specific DNA or RNA sequences, widely used in diagnostic testing for infectious diseases. PEG-IFN (Pegylated Interferon): A modified form of interferon with an attached polyethylene glycol molecule, which prolongs its half-life and enhances its therapeutic effects, commonly used in the treatment of hepatitis B and C. PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes): A framework used in evidence-based medicine to formulate clinical research questions and guide systematic reviews. PITC (Provider-Initiated Testing and Counselling): A healthcare approach where medical providers recommend and offer testing for specific conditions, such as HIV or hepatitis, during routine clinical visits. PMTCT (Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission): Interventions aimed at reducing the risk of transmitting infections like HIV or hepatitis B from a mother to her child during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding. PPV (Positive Predictive Value): The probability that a person with a positive test result truly has the disease or infection being tested for. PQ (WHO Prequalification): A process by the World Health Organization to assess the quality, safety, and efficacy of medical products, ensuring they meet global standards. PWID (People Who Inject Drugs): A population group at high risk for bloodborne infections such as HIV and hepatitis due to the use of shared or non-sterile injecting equipment. QA (Quality Assurance): A systematic process to ensure that healthcare services and products meet established standards of quality. QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year): A measure used in health economics to assess the value of medical interventions by combining the quantity and quality of life gained. QC (Quality Control): A set of procedures to ensure that laboratory tests and medical products consistently meet specified performance criteria. QI (Quality Improvement): A continuous process of identifying and implementing changes to improve healthcare services and outcomes. RBV (Ribavirin): An antiviral medication often used in combination with other drugs to treat chronic hepatitis C infection. RCT (Randomized Controlled Trial): A study design in which participants are randomly assigned to receive either the intervention being tested or a control, considered the gold standard for evaluating treatment efficacy. RDT (Rapid Diagnostic Test): A diagnostic tool that provides results within a short time frame, often less than 30 minutes, and is commonly used for point-of-care testing. RNA (Ribonucleic Acid): A nucleic acid molecule involved in various biological roles, including coding, decoding, and regulation of genes, and is the genetic material for some viruses. RR (Relative Risk): A measure used in epidemiology to compare the risk of a certain event occurring in two different groups. SOP (Standard Operating Procedure): A set of step-by-step instructions to ensure consistency and quality in performing specific tasks or procedures. SSA (Sub-Saharan Africa): A geographical region of Africa located south of the Sahara Desert, often referenced in global health due to its high burden of infectious diseases. STI (Sexually Transmitted Infection): Infections transmitted primarily through sexual contact, including HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, and chlamydia. SVR (Sustained Virological Response): The absence of detectable viral RNA in the blood at a defined time point after completing antiviral treatment, indicating successful treatment of hepatitis C. TDF (Tenofovir): An antiviral medication used to treat chronic hepatitis B and HIV infections. ULN (Upper Limit of Normal): The highest value within the normal reference range for a laboratory test. UNAIDS (Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS): A global initiative aimed at ending the HIV/AIDS epidemic through coordinated efforts in prevention, treatment, and advocacy. UNICEF (United Nations Children’s Fund): A United Nations agency dedicated to improving the health, education, and well-being of children worldwide. UNODC (United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime): A United Nations agency focused on addressing issues related to drug use, crime, and terrorism. VCT (Voluntary Counselling and Testing): A service where individuals voluntarily seek testing for infections like HIV, accompanied by preand post-test counselling. WHO (World Health Organization): A specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health. WHO GHP (WHO Global Hepatitis Programme): A WHO initiative focused on the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of hepatitis B and C infections globally. HBsAg (Hepatitis B Surface Antigen): A protein on the surface of the hepatitis B virus, detectable in the blood during acute and chronic hepatitis B infection. HBcAg (Hepatitis B Core Antigen): A protein found in the core of the hepatitis B virus, not typically detectable in serum due to its encapsulation by HBsAg. HBeAg (Hepatitis B e Antigen): A viral protein associated with high levels of hepatitis B virus replication, often used as a marker of active infection. Anti-HBs (Hepatitis B Surface Antibody): An antibody produced in response to hepatitis B vaccination or recovery from infection, indicating immunity. Anti-HBc (Hepatitis B Core Antibody): An antibody to the core protein of hepatitis B, detectable in both acute and chronic infections. Anti-HBc IgM: A subclass of anti-HBc antibodies, typically present in recent hepatitis B infections but may also be detected in chronic cases using sensitive assays. Anti-HBe (Hepatitis B e Antibody): An antibody to HBeAg, often indicating a lower level of viral replication. HBV DNA: The genetic material of the hepatitis B virus, detectable and quantifiable in serum using nucleic acid testing. Anti-HCV Antibody: An antibody to the hepatitis C virus, usually detectable in the blood within two to three months of infection or exposure. HCV RNA: The genetic material of the hepatitis C virus, detectable and quantifiable in serum using nucleic acid testing. HCV Core Antigen (HCVcAg): A nucleocapsid protein of the hepatitis C virus, detectable in plasma during viral assembly and throughout the course of infection. Chronic HBV Infection: Defined by the persistence of HBsAg for at least six months, confirmed by testing two specimens six months apart. Chronic HCV Infection: Characterized by the presence of HCV RNA or HCV core antigen in association with positive serology for HCV antibodies. Viraemic Infection: Refers to the presence of hepatitis B or C virus in the blood, indicating active or ongoing infection. Occult HBV Infection: A condition where HBsAg is undetectable, but HBV DNA is present at very low levels, often accompanied by anti-HBc positivity. Cirrhosis: An advanced stage of liver disease marked by extensive fibrosis, nodularity, and disrupted liver architecture and circulation. Decompensated Cirrhosis: A severe form of cirrhosis with clinical features such as portal hypertension, ascites, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, or liver insufficiency. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC): A primary liver cancer arising from hepatocytes, often a complication of chronic hepatitis B or C infection. HCV Sustained Virological Response (SVR): The absence of detectable HCV RNA in the blood at 12 or 24 weeks after completing treatment, indicating a cure. HCV Non-Response: The persistence of detectable HCV RNA in the blood throughout treatment. HCV Relapse: The reappearance of detectable HCV RNA after initially achieving undetectable levels during or at the end of treatment. HCV Viral Breakthrough: The reappearance of detectable HCV RNA during treatment after initially achieving undetectable levels. HBV Treatment Failure: Can be primary (failure to reduce HBV DNA by ≥1 log10 IU/mL within three months of therapy) or secondary (rebound of HBV DNA by ≥1 log10 IU/mL after an initial response). Serological Assays: Tests that detect antigens or antibodies in serum or plasma, commonly used for diagnosing hepatitis B and C. Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT): A quick immunoassay that detects antibodies or antigens, providing results in less than 30 minutes. Enzyme Immunoassay (EIA): Laboratory-based tests that detect antibodies, antigens, or both, often used for hepatitis diagnosis. Nucleic Acid Testing (NAT): A molecular technique, such as PCR, that detects and quantifies viral nucleic acids (RNA or DNA) with high sensitivity. Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The likelihood that a positive test result accurately indicates the presence of infection or disease. Negative Predictive Value (NPV): The likelihood that a negative test result accurately indicates the absence of infection or disease. Analytical Sensitivity/Limit of Detection (LoD): The lowest concentration of a substance that can be reliably detected in 95% of specimens under routine conditions. Testing Approaches: Include general population testing, focused testing of high-risk groups, birth-cohort testing, and antenatal clinic testing. Community-Based Testing: Testing conducted outside healthcare facilities, such as in homes, workplaces, schools, or through outreach campaigns. Facility-Based Testing: Testing conducted in healthcare settings, including primary care clinics, hospitals, and specialized clinics. Integration: The co-location and sharing of services across different disease areas, such as hepatitis, HIV, and tuberculosis. Decentralization: Delegating authority and resources to lower levels of the health system to improve service delivery. Task-Shifting/Sharing: Redistributing tasks from higher-level healthcare providers to trained lay providers. Lay Provider: A non-professionally certified individual trained to deliver specific healthcare services. Linkage to Care: A process to connect individuals diagnosed with hepatitis B or C to appropriate prevention, treatment, and care services. Global Burden of Disease: Chronic hepatitis B and C infections affect millions worldwide, with a disproportionate burden in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in Asia and Africa. Testing and Diagnosis: Early identification of chronic hepatitis B or C enables timely care and treatment, preventing disease progression and reducing transmission. WHO Guidelines: The first WHO guidelines on testing for chronic hepatitis B and C aim to strengthen and expand testing practices globally, particularly in low-resource settings.
